desc:
Place a binary tree on a complete binary tree frame: the root has slot 1, and a node in slot p has its left child in slot 2p and its right child in slot 2p + 1. The width of a level is (slot of its rightmost node) - (slot of its leftmost node) + 1 (missing nodes between the ends count), and the width of the tree is the largest width of any level.

You must choose exactly one node other than the root and cut it off together with its whole subtree. The remaining nodes keep their slots. Return the smallest tree width that can be reached by a single cut.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] the width is 4 (the last level, slots 4 to 7). Cutting node 4 leaves the slots 5, 6, 7 on the last level (width 3). Cutting node 2 removes 2, 4 and 5 and leaves the nodes 1, 3, 6, 7, whose levels have widths 1, 1 and 2, so the answer is 2. For tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, -1, -1, 5] the last level has slots 4 and 7 (width 4); cutting node 2 together with its child 4 leaves the single path 1, 3, 5, so the answer is 1.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
The tree has at most 30 levels, so every width fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Try every node as the one to cut, and think about how the widths of the levels change. Which levels are not affected at all?

Levels above the cut node keep their width. On every level below, the cut removes one contiguous block of nodes (the descendants of the cut node), and the width changes only if that block touches the left end or the right end of the level.

The descendants of a node on the next level form a block of consecutive positions that you can get from prefix counts of children. Walk down level by level while updating the block; the number of levels is at most 30, so O(n · levels) work is fine. Use prefix and suffix maxima of the original level widths for the levels above the cut and below the point where the block becomes empty.
editorial: Cutting a node removes, on each level below it, a contiguous block of nodes of that level (all the descendants of the cut node on that level, which stay together because levels are ordered left to right). If the block is strictly inside the level (there are nodes remaining on both sides), the leftmost and rightmost slots are unchanged, hence the width is unchanged. If the block contains the left end, the new width is measured from the first remaining node; symmetric for the right end; if the block is the whole level, the level disappears.

Index the nodes of each level 0..m-1 and store for each level the number of children produced by the first i nodes, childrenBefore[i]. Then the descendants of the block [a, b] on the next level are exactly the block [childrenBefore[a], childrenBefore[b+1] - 1]. For a cut node, start with its own one-element block on its level and walk down while the block is non-empty, recording the new width of each level. Levels above the cut are covered by a prefix maximum of the original widths, and once the block becomes empty the remaining deeper levels keep their original widths (a suffix maximum). The answer is the minimum over all cut nodes. Each node walks down at most as many levels as the tree has (at most 30), so the total time is O(n · L).
